one_liner: Rust WebAssembly runtime whose optional LLVM backend runs WASI code about 1.15x faster than Wasmtime and 1.34x faster than V8.
what_it_does: Wasmer is a WebAssembly runtime (CLI, Rust crate and C API, now marketed as a sandbox platform with its WASIX extensions) that compiles Wasm modules to native code through a pluggable compiler: Singlepass, Cranelift (the default) or LLVM. This entry covers the LLVM backend, chosen with `wasmer run --llvm` or by building a store with `Store::new(LLVM::new())` from the wasmer-compiler-llvm crate. Compiled modules can be serialized, cross-compiled and later loaded in headless mode without a compiler. Its API is Wasmer's own, not the Wasmtime embedding API or Node's WASI.
how_it_is_fast: Each Wasm function is lowered to its own LLVM IR module (via inkwell) and the functions are compiled in parallel on a rayon pool. Ordinary-size functions get a hand-picked function-level pass list (SCCP, early-CSE, SROA, aggressive-instcombine, jump threading, GVN, DSE, loop-rotate, indvars, memcpyopt), and code generation runs at OptimizationLevel::Aggressive with the host CPU's feature flags. Statically reserved linear memories rely on guard pages instead of explicit bounds compares (dynamic memories get a check marked likely-in-bounds with llvm.expect). Memory 0's base pointer is passed as a hidden first argument (the 'm0' or pass-params optimization, on by default since 7.1), and memory accesses carry per-memory TBAA tags. There is no cross-function inlining because each function is its own module, and functions above a size threshold drop to an O1-style pipeline; both cap how close it gets to whole-module LLVM AOT runtimes such as WAMR's wamrc, wasm2c or WAVM.
when_to_use: Long-running, CPU-bound WASI modules (crypto, codecs, numeric kernels) where steady-state throughput matters more than compile latency, and compiled modules can be cached or serialized.

You already embed Wasmer (Rust or C API, WASIX) on its default Cranelift backend: swapping in LLVM gave a 0.858x geomean time (about 1.17x) on the 2022-12 libsodium suite, or about 1.08-1.10x on the non-trivial rows (derived from page data).
Ahead-of-time pipelines: compile with LLVM on a build machine (cross-compilation is supported), ship the serialized artifact and run it headless without LLVM on the target.
x86-64 or aarch64 hosts on Linux, macOS or Windows where an LLVM 22 toolchain can be installed for the build.
when_not_to_use: Startup- or compile-latency-sensitive work (cold starts, untrusted uploads, blockchains): LLVM compiles far slower than Cranelift or Singlepass. Wasmer's own Singlepass README recommends Singlepass where JIT bombs are a risk, and the 7.1 changelog says huge functions had to drop optimization (Python compile time from about 90 s to about 10 s). A Wasmer 2.2 blog snippet (page blocked) describes a module where Cranelift took about 10 minutes and the LLVM compile was stopped after 3 hours.

When peak steady-state speed is the only goal: in the same 2022-12 data WAMR's iwasm (wasmer-llvm takes 1.277x its time, faster on 1 of 69 tests) and wasm2c (1.171x) are faster. WasmEdge is also faster on every row large enough to measure well (see gotchas).
Production use of Wasmer 6.0 or later with the LLVM backend when you are not a paying Wasmer sponsor: the crate is BUSL-1.1. The last MIT release of wasmer-compiler-llvm is 5.0.6 (2025-05-02).

SIMD-heavy or unusual store patterns: open issues report large LLVM-backend slowdowns for v128.bitselect feeding extends (#6535), i64x2 shifts by 32..63 (#6529), dynamic i8x16 shifts (#6521), store16 and rem_u-addressed stores (#6491, #6489), f64.convert_i64_u (#6083) and memory.size (#6147).
Code written against the Wasmtime embedding API or Node's WASI: this is a different runtime and API, not a drop-in replacement.

integration.form: crate (wasmer plus wasmer-compiler-llvm), C API library (lib/c-api), or the wasmer CLI
integration.dependencies: A system LLVM 22 install (llvm-config-22 on PATH or LLVM_SYS_221_PREFIX; on Debian also libpolly-22-dev); inkwell 0.10 and rayon; Cranelift is the default compiler when LLVM is not enabled
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.96 (workspace rust-version, edition 2024) and LLVM 22.1.x exactly
integration.platforms: The LLVM backend initializes targets for x86-64, aarch64, riscv64 and loongarch64. BUILD.md covers Linux, macOS and Windows (LLVM 22.1 installer). Prebuilt CLI assets exist for linux amd64/aarch64/riscv64, darwin arm64 and windows; the changelog says LLVM was added to the macOS ARM64 binaries in 5.0.1, but whether every prebuilt binary includes LLVM is not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Engine and Module are shared through cheap clones (cloning a Module is a shallow copy); every call takes &mut Store, so one thread drives a Store at a time. Compilation itself runs in parallel across functions (num_threads defaults to available_parallelism).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: inside Wasmer it is a one-line compiler swap (Store::new(LLVM::new()) or --llvm); against Wasmtime or V8 it is a different runtime with a different API

gotchas: Licence split: the repository and its badge say MIT, but wasmer-compiler-llvm and wasmer-compiler-singlepass from 6.0.0 (2025-04-24) are under the Business Source License 1.1 (crates.io lists them as 'non-standard'). Production use is allowed only for Wasmer sponsors; each version becomes MPL 2.0 four years after publication. The last MIT LLVM crate is 5.0.6 (2025-05-02). The benchmarked 2022 build was MIT-era (release dates suggest 3.0.x to 3.1.0; the version is not stated).
The build needs LLVM 22 exactly: BUILD.md says any other version silently disables the backend, so check the 'Enabled Compilers:' banner.

Semantics knobs: by default, user memory loads and stores on static memories are marked volatile so LLVM cannot delete them, which costs speed (issue #3987 shows a dead load emitted before each store). Non-volatile memops are faster but the code calls them 'not 100% SPEC compliant'; they are switched on automatically for WASIX modules (PR #6212), with --disable-non-volatile-memops to opt out. NaN canonicalization is off by default.

Harness flaw in the benchmark: about 18 of the 70 libsodium rows are tiny (values under 5000 for every runtime; onetimeauth2 is recorded as 0 or 1). The 2022 run's units and timer are undocumented: today's cmptest.h, with ITERATIONS=200 and a microsecond clock, could only print multiples of 5000. The wins over Wasmtime and V8 survive dropping those rows (0.841x and 0.753x on 51 rows at 5000 or above). The apparent geomean win over WasmEdge (0.819x on 69 rows, but faster on only 31) comes from the tiny rows: on rows at 5000 or above, wasmer-llvm takes 1.031x WasmEdge's time (faster on 15 of 51), and 1.104x on rows at 100000 or above. The first-party README claim of 'about 50% faster' than Cranelift is not reproduced: 0.858x wasmer-cranelift's time (about 1.17x faster) on 70 rows, 0.902x on rows at 5000 or above (all derived from page data).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Wasmtime and V8 (and over Wasmer's own Cranelift default) when you are already on Wasmer and want steady-state throughput on long-running modules. If peak throughput is the only goal, the WAMR (iwasm) and wasm2c siblings were faster on the same libsodium data. For startup-bound work, interpreters such as Wasmi, wasm3 or Fizzy are the right choice.
verified_claims_summary: Frank Denis's December 2022 run of libsodium's built-in benchmark suite compiled once to WASI (about 70 crypto primitives, the same wasm for every runtime, compile time excluded; per a snippet of his post, a Zen 2 CPU pinned to one core, with runtime versions and flags unstated) gives wasmer-llvm 0.872x Wasmtime's per-test time and 0.747x Node/V8's. These are geomeans over 69 shared tests, faster on 54 and 60 respectively (derived from page data). I reproduced both figures exactly from the CSVs; dropping the tiny rows gives 0.841x and 0.753x, and WAMR's iwasm and wasm2c stay faster than wasmer-llvm.
status_note: Actively maintained (7.5.0 released 2026-10-01, commits on 2026-10-06, 21.1k stars) and usable as a crate or CLI, but the LLVM backend's BUSL-1.1 licence since 6.0 limits production use to Wasmer sponsors unless you pin the MIT 5.0.6 release; the speedup was measured on a 2022 MIT-era build with undocumented units for the tiny rows.
